## Introduction

The goal of today's workshop is to explore data related to time.

Specifically we will:

- Explore multivariate techniques for dimension reduction
- Plot multivariate data

## Scenario

Characterized by low in situ primary production, sandy beaches are a classic example of subsidized ecosystems, maintaining food webs that rely fundamentally on inputs from adjacent habitats such as rocky reefs, kelp forests, and seagrass meadows. These marine subsidies in the form of detached macrophytes, support a high diversity and abundance of intertidal invertebrate consumers which in turn provide a critical energy source for higher-trophic level predators including surf zone fish. While several studies examine the effects of detached macrophytes in coastal environments only a few studies have attempted to investigate the influence of wrack inputs on sandy beach surf zone fish communities, particularly across large spatial scales, hindering our ability to develop more general inferences about the role of floating macrophytes in dynamic nearshore habitats. 

Here we investigate the relationship between floating macrophyte communities (wrack) and surf zone fish communities.


## Data citation

Jenifer Dugan, & Michelle Marraffini. (2026). California coast, ecosystem surveys of sandy beaches and surf zones (Long-term monitoring). California Ocean Protection Council Data Repository. urn:uuid:9ea66d7e-ddbe-4acc-a78e-902d6d19fd4b.

## Load data

Adjust paths to files as necessary on your machine

```{r}
fish_wrack <- read.csv("../data/func_fish_wide_wrack.csv")
glimpse(fish_wrack)
```
Columns:

- region: North, Central and South bioregions of California. Central:South boundary is Pt Conception a break in many many marine species ranges. Only two sites in the North were sampled

- site_name: Beach site name

- site_pair: pair is one MPA and one reference site with similar biophysical characteristics

- mpa_status: MPA or reference site 

- num_sites: count of site (internal data qa/qc) ignore

- brown - animal indicate wrack groupings

- Agonidae - Squatinidae indicate fish family or functional groups


### Check data

Multivariate techniques can struggle when columns and/or rows of the matrix have know observations

```{r}
# Surveys were no shorebirds were observed
rownames(fish_wrack[, 5:25])[rowSums(fish_wrack[, 5:25]) == 0]

# Species that were never observed, this should equal 0 since we filtered the data before pivoting above
colnames(fish_wrack[, 5:25])[colSums(fish_wrack[, 5:25]) == 0]
```

in this data these have already been filtered but it is usually a good idea to double check. 

Some analyses can also struggle with rare species/groups so the code above can be adjusted to some other threshold.

## PCA for dimension reduction
Let's look only at the fish for a minute

```{r}
# we use 'scale. = TRUE' in prcomp to ensures variables with 
# different units or scales are comparable. but ours are all species counts
fish_pca <- prcomp(fish_wrack[, 13:25])

# View the summary to see how much variance is explained by each component.
# This helps identify the "meaningful components".
summary(fish_pca)
```

### Let's look at the PCs

```{r}
# How much proportion of the variance is explained by each PC. The importance
pc_var <- round(summary(fish_pca)$importance[2, 1:2] * 100, 1)

# Add categorical variables
pca_data <- data.frame(fish_pca$x, Site = fish_wrack$site_name, mpa_status = fish_wrack$mpa_status)

# Each original variable has an specific contribution to each PC, this are called loadings
pca_loadings <- as.data.frame(fish_pca$rotation)

pca_loadings
```


### PCA plot

```{r, echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
# Create a biplot to represent both the observations (points)
pca_data |> 
ggplot() +
  aes(x = PC1, y = PC2) +
  geom_point(aes(color = Site), size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA Ordination: ",
    subtitle = "Projecting 374 variables into 2 dimensions",
    x = paste0("PC1 (", pc_var[1], "% variance)"),
    y = paste0("PC2 (", pc_var[2], "% variance)")
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  # How does each variable relate to the ordination of the points?
  geom_segment(data = pca_loadings, 
               aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1*2, yend = PC2*2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), 
               color = "black", 
               linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = pca_loadings,
            aes(x = PC1*2.1, y = PC2*2.1, label = row.names(pca_loadings)))


```
Well that's not helpful

## Hellinger transformation

Hellinger transformation is used in many un-even community datasets, to better linearize the distances among sites (and reduce the effect of dominant species in the site dissimilarity) (Legendre and Legendre, 2012)


```{r, echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
func_Fish_sp_hel <- decostand(fish_wrack[, c(13:25)], method = "hellinger", na.rm = T)

scale_wrack <- scale(fish_wrack[,6:10])
```


## PCA plot with transformation

```{r}
fish_pca2 <- prcomp(func_Fish_sp_hel)

pc_var <- round(summary(fish_pca2)$importance[2, 1:4] * 100, 1)

fish_pca_loadings <- as.data.frame(fish_pca2$rotation)

pca_data2 <- data.frame(fish_pca2$x, regions = fish_wrack$region, 
                        sites = fish_wrack$site_pair, 
                        status = fish_wrack$mpa_status)



p12 <- ggplot(pca_data2, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = regions, shape = status), size = 3, alpha = 0.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PC1 (", pc_var[1], "% variance)"),
    y = paste0("PC2 (", pc_var[2], "% variance)")
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  geom_segment(data = fish_pca_loadings, 
               aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1*2, yend = PC2*2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), 
               color = "black", 
               linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = fish_pca_loadings,
            aes(x = PC1*2.1, y = PC2*2.1, label = row.names(fish_pca_loadings)))+
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = sites), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE)

# PC2 vs 3
p23 <- ggplot(pca_data2, aes(x = PC2, y = PC3)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = regions, shape = status), size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PC2 (", pc_var[2], "% variance)"),
    y = paste0("PC3 (", pc_var[3], "% variance)")
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  geom_segment(data = fish_pca_loadings, 
               aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC2*2, yend = PC3*2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), 
               color = "black", 
               linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = fish_pca_loadings,
            aes(x = PC2*2.1, y = PC3*2.1, label = row.names(fish_pca_loadings)))+
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = sites), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE)



HPCA <- p12 + p23 + plot_layout(ncol = 2, widths = unit(c(7, 7), c("cm", "cm")))

HPCA

```

## Two multivariate datasets

Now let's explore more of the data. We have data on wrack and fish.

## Cluster analysis

```{r}
# stick with hellinger transformation for both matrices
# since they are separate data, transform them separately
# func_Fish_sp_hel
wrack_hel <- as.data.frame(decostand(fish_wrack[,6:10], method = "hellinger", na.rm = T))

Fish_wrack_hel <- cbind(wrack_hel, func_Fish_sp_hel)

row.names(Fish_wrack_hel) <- fish_wrack$site_name

```


## K means

How many clusters?

`cascadeKM()` function in `vegan` package has two options for methods of assessing number of clusters.


```{r}
# cascadeKM() inside vegan
KM <- cascadeKM(Fish_wrack_hel, 2, 6, iter = 25, criterion = "ssi")
  
plot(KM, , sortg = T)
```
**ssi**:

the “Simple Structure Index” multiplicatively combines several elements which influence the interpretability of a partitioning solution. The best partition is indicated by the highest SSI value.

```{r}
# cascadeKM() inside vegan
KM <- cascadeKM(Fish_wrack_hel, 2, 6, iter = 25, criterion = "calinski")
  
plot(KM, , sortg = T)
```
**calinski**:

(SSB/(K-1)) / (SSW/(n-k))

where n is the number of data points and k is the number of clusters. SSW is the sum of squares within the clusters while SSB is the sum of squares among the clusters. This index is simply an F (ANOVA) statistic.

SSI suggest 4 clusters and calinski suggests 3 clusters.


## K = 4

Let's start with 4 clusters and see what that looks like.

```{r}
set.seed(123)

Fish_wrack_KM_4 <- kmeans(Fish_wrack_hel, centers = 4)

table(row.names(Fish_wrack_hel), Fish_wrack_KM_4$cluster)
```
Table illustrates which sites are in which cluster.

```{r}
Clusters_biplot <- fviz_cluster(Fish_wrack_KM_4,
                   data = Fish_wrack_hel,
                   repel = T)


Clusters_biplot
```
Cluster 3 seems odd. It is made up of 3 sites Percos, Whalers Cove, and Stillwater Cove. But is seems to touch cluster 4 at Greyhound Rock.


```{r}
HeatMap <- heatmap(Fish_wrack_KM_4$centers, 
           main = "Cluster profiles (Hellinger-transformed)")
```
The heat map allows us to explore which fish and algae make up each cluster. 

How to read it: each column is a variable. Each observation is a row. Each square is a value. High values are drawn in red and low values in yellow, by default. 

This default map is a little busy, let's remove the dendrograms

```{r}
heatmap(Fish_wrack_KM_4$centers, Colv = NA, Rowv = NA,
           main = "Cluster profiles (Hellinger-transformed)")
```
That is simpler. 

### Colors

Base R has some native color palettes: terrain.color(), rainbow(), heat.colors(), topo.colors() or cm.colors()

```{r}
heatmap(Fish_wrack_KM_4$centers, Colv = NA, Rowv = NA, col = terrain.colors(128),
           main = "Cluster profiles (Hellinger-transformed)")
```


Alternatively you can use color palettes from other libraries
```{r}
library(RColorBrewer)
coul <- colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(8, "PiYG"))(25)
heatmap(Fish_wrack_KM_4$centers, Colv = NA, Rowv = NA, col = coul,
           main = "Cluster profiles (Hellinger-transformed)")
```



```{r}
# Use 'scale' to normalize
# our data was already scaled/clustered so this is not appropriate for our data
heatmap(Fish_wrack_KM_4$centers, Colv = NA, Rowv = NA, 
        col = terrain.colors(128), scale="column",  
           main = "Cluster profiles (Hellinger-transformed)")
```

By default (scale = "row") the rows are scaled to have mean zero and standard deviation one.

### Interpretation
Here I am using the original colors, but have flipped the chart so we can read the fish labels easier.

To do this I had to flip the matrix and flip the `scale` argument.

```{r}
heatmap(t(Fish_wrack_KM_4$centers), Colv = NA, Rowv = NA, scale = "column",
           main = "Cluster profiles (Hellinger-transformed)")
```

For wrack groups, brown is pretty high in all clusters. Seagrass appears highest in cluster 1 and lowest in cluster 4. 

For fish: some fish are equally rare in all clusters. Surf specialists are higher in clusters 1, 2, & 4. Sciaenidae is only high in cluster 1. Reef associated is high in cluster 3.

## RDA


```{r}
# made transformed data earlier
func_fish_wrack_RDA_2 <- rda(func_Fish_sp_hel ~ . , data = as.data.frame(scale_wrack))
anova(func_fish_wrack_RDA_2, permutations = 999)

```

```{r}
# look at algae groups
anova.cca(func_fish_wrack_RDA_2, by = "margin", permutations = 999)
```

```{r}
# consider site pairs as blocks
h <- how(blocks = fish_wrack$site_pair)

anova.cca(func_fish_wrack_RDA_2, by = "margin", permutations = h) # none significative

vif.cca(func_fish_wrack_RDA_2)

adj_r2_2 <- RsquareAdj(func_fish_wrack_RDA_2)$adj.r.squared
adj_r2_2
```


No algae significant for explaining fish composition by functional groups with very little variance explained (`r adj_r2_2`)


```{r}
#get data
site_data_RDA <- as.data.frame(scores(func_fish_wrack_RDA_2, display = "sites"))

fish_data_RDA <- as.data.frame(scores(func_fish_wrack_RDA_2, display = "species"))

algae_data_RDA <- as.data.frame(scores(func_fish_wrack_RDA_2, display = "bp"))

# organise to plot
RDA_plot_df <- data.frame(site_data_RDA,
                          site = as.factor(fish_wrack$site_name), 
                          region = as.factor(fish_wrack$region))

# Projection
legend_text <- paste0(row.names(RDA_plot_df), ". ", RDA_plot_df$site, collapse = "\n")
```


```{r}

RDA_plot <- RDA_plot_df |>  ggplot() +
  # sites as points
  geom_point(aes(x = RDA1, y = RDA2, color = region),size = 1) +
  annotate("label", x = Inf, y = Inf, label = legend_text,
    hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.25))) +
  geom_text(aes(x = RDA1, y = RDA2,label = row.names(RDA_plot_df), nudge_x = 0.05))+

  # fish families/funct groups as blue arrows
  geom_segment(data = fish_data_RDA, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = RDA1, yend = RDA2), 
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")), color = "blue") +
  geom_text(data = fish_data_RDA, aes(x = RDA1, y = RDA2, label = rownames(fish_data_RDA)), 
            color = "darkblue", size = 3, check_overlap = TRUE, position = position_jitter()) +
  # wrack as green arrows
  geom_segment(data = algae_data_RDA, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = RDA1, yend = RDA2), 
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = algae_data_RDA, aes(x = RDA1, y = RDA2, label = rownames(algae_data_RDA)), #orchid4
            color = "darkgreen", fontface = "bold", check_overlap = TRUE) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "RDA: Fish functional group Predicted by Algae type",
       subtitle = paste("Proportion Inertia Constrained =", round(adj_r2_2, 3))) #, round(adj_r2, 3))

RDA_plot
```

Seagrass seems to be associated with Scianidae on the South, considering the marginal significance. Is interesting how the surf specialist "goes away" from all the wrack types, specially Green.
